                 Abstract
                 This paper presents a study on the risk associated with CO2 injection in geological storage and fault
                 reactivation through a comprehensive workflow for determining the feasibility of CO2 storage campaign in
                 carbonate reservoir in Malaysia. The study includes constructing a 4-D coupled reservoir geomechanical
                 model and developing a workflow that can be used to evaluate geomechanics risks associated with carbon
                 capture and storage (CCS) by outlining results and findings that drive key decisions in the planning of CCS
                 strategy.
                    The workflows aims to better delineate and enumerate the risks with CCS as it constructing and
                 calibrating single well models by corroborating numerous inputs including stringent laboratory testing data
                 and drilling analysis, and combining with structural model and reservoir model to create a field wide 4-D
                 geomechanical model using advanced time lapsed geomechanics simulation. Coupled simulations with the
                 dynamic reservoir model provided predictions of the fault stability by considering fault deformation. The
                 paper further highlights the geomechanics evaluation consideration (economics and engineering trade-off)
                 in designing maximum safe injection pressure for CO2 sequestration program.
                    The results of the study show fault condition subjected to different time-steps of the coupled simulation
                 during depletion and injection. At each time-step, the development of plastic shear strain and absolute
                 displacement are plotted and risks associated with the change in reservoir pressure are assessed and
                 quantified. Different injection plans are modelled to determine the impact on final storage capacity, long
                 term fluid containment and upper safe injection limit to avoid breaching the caprock.
                    The study offers the utilization of the latest techniques in 4-D coupled geomechanical modelling which
                 reduced the study time and cost significantly, making it affordable for in-time solution for decision making.
                 The paper also aims to encourage the consideration of the applied novel workflow involved in CCS strategye
                 valuation focusing on risk assessment which ultimately will affect reservoir maximum safe injection limit,
                 capacity, long term storage safety, and monitoring program to mitigate potential geohazard leakage.

                 Introduction
                 The carbonate formations in the Central Luconia province offshore Sarawak, Malaysia generally form
                 prolific gas producing reservoirs. The field being studies is operated by PETRONAS and is located as
                 shown in Figure 1. The field is primarily of platform type carbonate build-up with a single long gas
                 column overlying an aquifer, and the field production started in 1995. GPS surveillance data, measured on
                 the platform over the past 20 years, have clearly shown a number of striking events related to reservoir
                 compaction and seabed subsidence, as a result of the gas production.
                    Currently PETRONAS is planning to use the field for CO2 injection and storage from nearby high CO2
                 content gas producing fields. It is therefore important to understand the geomechanics-related risks such
                 as subsidence and uneven lateral movement, fault reactivation, and cap rock integrity associated with the
                 long term CO2 storage design strategy.
                    A 4-D coupled reservoir geomechanical study has been conducted to model the pore collapse behavior
                 of the carbonate reservoir in the field, calibrate the model with the field measured data, forecast the long
                 term seabed subsidence and lateral movement, and also to study the risks associated with CO2 injection
                 with long term storage.

                 Methodology
                 In order to better delineate and enumerate the risks of CO2 sequestration, a novel and inclusive workflow
                 (Figure 2) is implemented which includes constructing validated 1-D geomechanical models together with
                 comprehensive laboratory testing programme, incorporating specialized creep tests. The validated 1-D
                 models were combined with structural model and reservoir model to create a field wide 4-D geomechanical
                 model using advanced time-lapsed coupled geomechanical simulations. The finite element simulations
                 coupled with the dynamic reservoir model provided predictions of the caprock seal integrity and fault
                 behavior for the proposed injection scenario by considering shear damage and plastic strains of the seal
                 and faults.

                 1-D Mechanical Earth Model
                 1-D Mechanical Earth Model (1-D MEM) consists of 3 main components which includes in-situ stresses,
                 rock mechanical properties and pore pressure along the well. It contains all the relevant geomechanics
                 information for any geomechanics-related applications such as wellbore stability analysis, sand production
                 prediction, caprock integrity assessment, fault stability assessment and compaction and subsidence
                 evaluation. Well calibrated 1-D MEMs are essential as a solid foundation for robust geomechanics analyses.
                 Good quality MEM should be able to explain observed drilling experiences with the modelling results.
                    Four validated 1-D MEMs were selected for the 3-D model construction namely X-1, X-2, X-3 and
                 X-4. The selection criteria are mainly based on data availability (sonic log) and log quality. Rock elastic
                 properties were derived based on sonic logs and conversion from dynamic to static elastic properties was
                 conducted to achieve good match with rock mechanics test data. Rock strength properties were derived
                 from in-house correlations of the region. Emphasis is placed on lithology identification whereby different
                 correlations were applied to different lithologies and to match the wellbore stability predictions with the
                 drilling experiences.
                    Poroelastic horizontal strain method was used to predict and capture the variability of horizontal stresses
                 in different lithologies and formation. The minimum horizontal stress magnitude was calibrated against
                 leak-off test (LOT) data while the stress azimuth was inferred from compilation of regional stress map in
                 Sarawak Basin (Tjia, 1994). Stress regime understanding from the region is normal stress regime transitional
                 to strike slip regime near top of carbonate and in the carbonate section. Horizontal stress anisotropy is small
                 which is consistent with regional knowledge.
                    These data are then used for the following in constructing 3-D geomechanical model:

                           • Derive rock mechanical elastic and strength property correlations with porosity for population in
                             reservoir.
                           • Determine control points for tectonic stress boundary condition used for 3-D stress initialization.
                           • Populate overburden rock properties.
                           • Populate overburden pore pressure (pore pressure in the reservoir is from dynamic model).
                   One of the 1-D MEMs is shown in Figure 3. Log track from left to right are lithology code (sand, shale
                 and carbonate), well inclination and azimuth, rock elastic properties, rock strength properties, pore pressure
                 and total principal in-situ stresses, mud weight window gradient, bit size and caliper, and casing shoe depth.

                 3-D Geomechanical Model
                 The dynamic reservoir model was used as the basis for construction of the 3-D geomechanical model. The
                 geomechanical model in the reservoir and aquifer zones was extended to seabed (overburden), sideburden
                 and underburden (Figure 4). Extra effort was made to ensure smooth transition between reservoir grid and
                 embedded grid to assist in subsequent numerical computation (Figure 5). The boundary condition was set
                 orthogonal to the maximum horizontal stress direction (20 degrees from North). The total number of grid
                 cells of the embedded 3-D geomechanical model is approximately 2 million cells.

                 Rock Mechanical Properties Population
                 The 3-D distribution of density, elastic properties and rock strength properties in the reservoir section were
                 based on porosity correlations as shown in Table 1. It is observed the rock exhibits pore collapse failure
                 during pore pressure depletion in uniaxial pore volume compressibility (UPVC) tests based onp-q plot and
                 porosity vs. volumetric strain plot. Thus, ISAMGEO chalk model (Plischke, 1994) incorporating creeping
                 is used for this field to cater for the cap failure and creeping behavior (evidence from GPS). The model
                 parameters are established based on numerical simulation of UPVC tests with actual laboratory test stress
                 path and subsequently, correlations were derived against sample porosity (Table 2).

                 Stress Boundary Condition initialization
                 Initialization of in-situ stresses is inferred from 1-D Mechanical Earth Model whereby iterative boundary
                 conditions were applied until reasonable match between 3-D geomechanical model and 1-D MEM stresses
                 is achieved. The calculation of a representative pre-production stress distribution relied on the consideration
                 of gravity and pore pressure forces acting internally within the model as well as an external horizontal
                 loading scheme acting on the vertical model boundaries.
                    The stress boundary condition of the model is tabulated in Table 3.
                    The maximum horizontal stress orientation adopted for this field is N20°E based on the stress orientation

                 Stress-step Selection
                 The reservoir pressure model at pre-production and subsequent stress-steps were selected based on average
                 field reservoir pressure of history-matched dynamic model. The reservoir pressure data at the selected time-
                 steps were used as inputs to compute the stresses and strains in the reservoir and surrounding formations.
                 Phase 1 represents the production phase, Phase 2 represents the end of production period (increase in
                 pressure is due to strong aquifer drive), and Phase 3 represents the beginning of CO2 injection period. Figure
                 7 shows a total of 23 selected stress-steps for the study. Emphasis (more stress-steps) were selected during
                 reservoir depletion and aquifer support phase as GPS measurement data were available during this period
                 whereby a smoother subsidence can be captured for comparison with the GPS data.

                 Subsidence and reservoir compaction from depletion
                 At the end of depletion in Year 2003, seabed subsidence is predicted to be approximately 9.6ft, which
                 then continues due to creep effect. The maximum subsidence predicted is approximately 11.3ft in Year
                 2013 which is consistent with GPS measurement in 2014 of approximately 11.65ft. Once CO2 injection
                 is initiated in Year 2024, the reservoir experienced additional pressure support which resulted in seabed
                 uplift of approximately 1ft. At the end of the injection scenario, a maximum seabed subsidence of 10.6ft
                 and reservoir compaction of 16ft were predicted as shown in Figure 9. Iterative calibration of pore collapse
                 and creep parameters from laboratory test data range was conducted to achieve reasonable to good match
                 against subsidence from GPS measurements of platform. Figure 10 shows the aerial view comparison of
                 seabed bathymetry survey from 2002 and 2012 against the model predictions. The subsidence bowl was
                 observed to be qualitatively consistent at North-West of the platform location.

                 Fault Stability Analysis
                 Numerical fault stability analysis utilizing frictional element is among one of the approaches adopted in the
                 industry. With the use of critical state failure model (ISAMGEO), plastic strain is unable to be computed
                 along the frictional elements (Mohr Coulomb failure criteria). Therefore, a workaround is implemented
                 whereby the results of fault deformation along the fault surface were interpreted to assess the fault
                 reactivation potential.
                    Another challenge in fault stability modeling is the lack of fault mechanical properties as rock sample
                 is not commonly taken from a fault. In order to estimate suitable fault mechanical properties, a literature
                 review was conducted as summarized in Table 4. From this investigation, a wide range of fault mechanical
                 properties has been used in different fields for fault stability study. In this study, the approach and fault
                 properties discussed by Khodarverdian, et al. (2014) was adopted as it was conducted in offshore Sabah
                 which is regionally close to Sarawak where the field is located.

                 Conclusions
                 The feasibility study on CO2 injection and storage in Field X using 4-D coupled geomechanical modelling
                 generates the following findings:

                           • Comparison of seabed subsidence data obtained from GPS measurements up to 2014 with predicted
                             subsidence are in good agreement.
                           • The modelling suggests 10.6ft of seabed subsidence and 16ft of reservoir compaction at the end
                             of injection scenario in Year 2040.
                           • Localized reservoir rock failure based on plastic strain was observed at the crest of the reservoir.
                           • Current depletion and proposed injection scheme could result in limited fault deformation in the
                             order of 0.5cm at five overburden bounding faults.
                           • The recommended maximum allowable injection reservoir pressure is 4000psi with 600psi
                             extended safety margin in order to minimize the risk for generation of sub-vertical fracture at the
                             cap rock considering stress changes and plastic strains based on compaction, subsidence, cap rock
                             integrity and fault stability analyses.
                    The study offers the utilization of the latest techniques in 4-D coupled geomechanical modelling hence
                 reduced the study time and costs significantly, making it affordable for in-time solutions for decision
                 making. The paper also aims to encourage the community and industry to consider the workflow involved in
                 CCS strategy evaluation, focusing on risk assessment which ultimately will affect reservoir maximum safe
